role: Lead AI Platform Engineer — Wolters Kluwer, Platform Engineering Team (via Andela; recruiter Paul Abbott)
source: August-2026/26/wolters-kluwer-principal-ai-platform-engineer/Wolters Kluwer Lead AI Platform Engineer JD India.pdf
scored_against: LEAD bars — 7+ yrs total, 5+ production Python, 4+ Web APIs, 3+ cloud, 2+ GenAI, 3+ SDK, 3+ CI/CD, 4+ SQL/NoSQL
binding_constraint: Production Python duration — 14 months (Mar 2025 - Apr 2026) against a 5+ year stated minimum. A CAPABILITY CAP of the duration kind: no rewrite, no Rule 7 re-vectoring and no generous reading closes it. Second constraint: SDK packaging, semantic versioning and PyPI/registry distribution, unevidenced anywhere in the record against a 3+ year minimum.
smallest_honest_lift: None exists for the score. Rule 7 re-vectoring of the Amura work would make the fourteen months read as densely as they deserve and would improve how a human reads him — it cannot add elapsed years. Do not fabricate to reach 95.
recommended_level: PRINCIPAL — despite scoring 5.1 points lower, because the binding constraint is identical on both documents and every differentiator he has is priced into the Principal document and priced out of the Lead one. See verdict.

scores.criterion: production-python-duration-and-depth — "7+ years of professional software development experience, including 5+ years of hands-on production Python" (Lead JD, Experience and Skills Required, bullet 1)
scores.evidence:
SPLIT VERDICT — the first half of the bullet is cleared by a wide margin; the second half is not met.

TOTAL EXPERIENCE — MET, and far past the bar. professional-journey.md line 38: "Total span: 19+ years, Apr 2007 -> Apr 2026." The timeline table (lines 22-37) carries all ten employers with dates. 19+ against a 7+ bar.

PRODUCTION PYTHON — NOT MET. His production Python is one continuous window: VoltusWave 2nd stint, Principal Software Architect, Mar 2025 - Apr 2026 (professional-journey.md line 37). That is FOURTEEN MONTHS against a 60-month bar — 23% of the requirement.

What those fourteen months actually contain is senior-grade and should not be undersold. professional-journey.md line 678: "10-query decision-intelligence platform in Python (FastAPI, LangChain, LangGraph) with 4 reusable archetypes." killer-query-case-studies/ documents it across ten case studies: FastAPI retrieval and calibration services with auth-resolved tenancy, Pydantic structured output, DuckDB + Parquet cohort builders, a DynamoDB event spine with a deterministic parquet snapshot exporter, propensity matching with standardised-mean-difference balance gates, seeded cluster-aware bootstrap CIs, and a 90-day outcome labeller shared across every cohort query in the programme. master/upgrad_resume.html section 6 carries four Amura bullets from this work.

DJANGO — claimable but unevidenced in depth. Django appears on the safe-to-claim list in CLAUDE.md line 132 (user-confirmed) and NOWHERE in professional-journey.md or killer-query-case-studies/. Verified by grep across the repo: the only hit outside a workspace is the CLAUDE.md safe-to-claim line itself. Claim Django as a framework he has used; do not attach years or a system to it.
scores.gaps:
1. THE DURATION, and it is the whole story. 14 months of production Python against "5+ years of hands-on production Python". Nothing in the record moves this number. There is no earlier Python role: the journey doc's cross-cutting threads (lines 74-95) place Python nowhere before the VoltusWave 2nd stint, and the nine prior employers are Java, .NET, Node/TypeScript, Go and SQL.
2. Django has no system, no employer and no duration behind it — one user-confirmed line and nothing else. Do not build an answer on it.
3. Python-ecosystem tooling (pytest, ruff, black, mypy) is absent from the entire corpus — scored separately under cicd-testing-and-quality-tooling.
scores.ramp_vs_cap:
CAPABILITY CAP — and specifically a DURATION cap, which is the one kind no rewrite, no re-vectoring and no Rule 7 pass can close. He cannot acquire 2025 Python years in 2026. This is the binding constraint on the whole rubric and it is identical on the Principal document (8+ years), where the same 14 months lands at 15% of the bar instead of 23%.

The honest framing for a room, which is NOT a score adjustment: he is a nineteen-year systems architect whose Python is one year old and whose Python output in that year was ten production services with statistical rigour, tenant isolation and leakage-safe machine learning. That is a real answer to "can you do the work". It is not an answer to "do you have five years", and the two questions should never be blurred together.
scores.verdict: 5/10. Half credit is the honest read: the engineering capability is present, current and deep, and the duration requirement is missed by 46 months. Read generously per the 'e.g. / or / preferably' rule this would score higher — but "5+ years of hands-on production Python" is not an 'e.g.' qualifier, it is a stated minimum, and inflating it would be exactly the fabrication the rules forbid.

scores.criterion: web-apis-in-python-at-scale — "4+ years building and operating Web APIs at scale using FastAPI, Django or Flask, including OpenAPI/Swagger and contract-first design" (Lead JD, bullet 2); responsibility 1: "Architect and implement secure, scalable Web APIs in Python using frameworks such as FastAPI, including authentication and authorisation, rate limiting and observability"
scores.evidence:
THE API-ARCHITECTURE CAPABILITY IS PAST THE BAR BY A DECADE. THE PYTHON-FRAMEWORK CLOCK IS NOT.

FastAPI in production, and it is not shallow. killer-query-case-studies/kq1-precedent-search.html: "FastAPI — The retrieval service, a single authenticated retrieval endpoint, auth-resolved tenancy." kq7-confidence-calibration.html: "FastAPI — The calibration service: role-resolved views, audit-first serving, canonical cache keys, tenant assertion on every cell", with the request path drawn as "FastAPI calibration service -> RBAC + audit -> LRU cache -> Tenant assertion per cell". FastAPI is named in the stack table of all ten case studies. Pydantic structured output appears in every stack line. That covers the responsibility's "authentication and authorisation" clause outright.

WEB APIs AT SCALE OUTSIDE PYTHON — fifteen-plus years, and directly transferable. master/live_card_dump_august_master.json PR-child-1 (Deque, Dec 2019 - Feb 2025) bullet 2: "Designed shared platform APIs on a multi-tenant SaaS — Jira integration + enterprise system contracts secured 20+ enterprise clients, with strict backward-compatibility discipline"; bullet 8: "Designed customer-specific frontends that called a shared Spring Boot backend with API versioning"; bullet 6: "Raised Application Programming Interface (API) quality for 20+ enterprise-client Software as a Service (SaaS), coaching engineers on documentation, code review, and scalable contracts." PR-child-2 (Rocket, 2018-19) bullets 1-2: REST APIs out of the IBM Db2 Configuration Manager decomposition. PR-child-6 (innRoad): "Productized REST-based WCF services that enabled and monetised customer integrations."

AT SCALE, literally: professional-journey.md line 649 describes the chat platform flow where "a single message will result in 50 external calls", corroborated at 48-58 calls per message by GROUNDING.md (line 652).

MIXED, and the split matters.

CAPABILITY CAP: the "4+ years using FastAPI, Django or Flask" clause. Fourteen months, unclosable.

RAMP ITEMS: OpenAPI/Swagger generation, contract-first tooling and rate limiting. These are days of work for someone who has already run backward-compatibility discipline across 20+ enterprise clients — the hard part of contract-first is the organisational discipline, and that he has been doing since 2019.
scores.verdict: 6/10. The API-design capability the seat actually needs is several times the stated bar; the Python-framework tenure is 29% of it. Six is the point where those two facts meet honestly.

scores.criterion: production-genai-llm-rag-and-evaluation — "2+ years of hands-on Generative AI experience in production or pre-production, including prompt engineering, LLM integration, RAG pipelines and model or response evaluation" (Lead JD, bullet 4); responsibility 5: LLMs and RAG, embeddings and vector stores, prompt design, evaluation and guardrails

RAG, in production. master/upgrad_resume.html section 6: "Engineered a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline on Elasticsearch dense_vector filtered nearest-neighbour search across 80+ chronic conditions, keeping Amazon Neptune off the serving path." kq1-precedent-search.html names Elasticsearch "the authoritative serving index — dense_vector filtered kNN plus denormalised precedent-card payloads" and Redis as a "Two-tier cache (final results + query embeddings) on canonical keys, with single-flight owner-token locks".

LLM INTEGRATION AND SELF-HOSTING. master/upgrad_resume.html section 6: "Secured protected health information inside the client virtual private cloud by self-hosting embeddings and Llama 3.1 for every model call." kq1 stack: "self-hosted Llama 3.1 (8B/70B)" served through Ollama inside the VPC. kq10-cross-domain.html: "traffic clears on the free 8B; only the tail the gate flags as uncertain escalates to 70B, and every routing decision is auditable code" — that is cost/latency-aware model routing, one of the Nice-to-Haves.

FRAMEWORKS. LangChain and LangGraph appear across the corpus (LangChain in 6 of 10 case studies, LangGraph in 4). kq1 architecture: "LangGraph runtime, Postgres checkpoints" and "LangChain, model seam — One provider door returning a BaseChatMod[el]". master/live_card_dump_august_master.json PR-child-0 bullet 12: "Launched 10-query decision-intelligence platform across 4 reusable archetypes (Retrieval, Cohort Aggregation, Sequence Mining, Graph Traversal)."

GUARDRAILS AND EVALUATION. "guardrail" appears 62 times across the case studies, "golden set" 21 times, offline eval 4 times. kq7 pipeline stage 9: "Eval + golden replay + alarm routing." Card bullet 15: "Deployed large language model narrative guardrails — pinned model + temperature=0 + chain hash + field-level claim grammar." 3. FORBIDDEN NUMBERS — kq2-outcome-correlation.html's served-cell table (412 / 217 / 0.58 / 0.34 / +24pp / max SMD 0.08) is labelled in the source as "Illustrative response shape, not a production measurement". 4. OPEN CLAIM, HIS CALL ALONE — whether the large language model narrative guardrails shipped. professional-journey.md line 681 asks it directly. KQ1's claim grammar is live; KQ9's shared contract is unsigned and its narrator ships off by default. Not resolved here, and not resolvable by any agent.

scores.ramp_vs_cap: DURATION SHORTFALL, not a capability cap. Every named capability in the bullet — prompt engineering, LLM integration, RAG pipelines, response evaluation — is evidenced in production. Only the clock is short, by roughly ten months. Bedrock and Azure OpenAI are RAMP ITEMS on the serving layer; he has run the harder version of the same problem (in-VPC self-hosted inference under HIPAA constraints).
scores.verdict: 8/10. His strongest technical criterion after the AI-assisted-development line. Two points off for a 10-month duration shortfall against a bar he nearly meets, and for a serving stack that shares no named product with the JD's preferred one.

scores.criterion: ai-assisted-development — "Demonstrated daily use of AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor or Claude Code, with concrete examples of productivity gains and the guardrails applied" (Lead JD, bullet 5); "Your Skills — AI-Assisted Pro"; responsibility 3
scores.evidence:
THE RAREST THING HE HAS, AND IT ANSWERS THIS LINE ALMOST WORD FOR WORD.

professional-journey.md line 669: "Embedded Claude Code + OpenAI Codex across the ~20-engineer team — daily architectural exploration, first-cut implementations, test scaffolding, all under hands-on review." master/live_card_dump_august_master.json PR-child-0 bullet 1 is the same claim on the live card. master/upgrad_resume.html section 6: "Drove a measured Claude Code and OpenAI Codex rollout across a 20-engineer team, covering first-cut implementation and test scaffolding under review."

The JD asks for three things and the record supplies two of them outright:
- DAILY USE of a named tool — yes, and the tool is one of the three the JD names by name.
- GUARDRAILS APPLIED — yes, and it is the load-bearing clause: "all under hands-on review". Scope was deliberately bounded to architectural exploration, first-cut implementations and test scaffolding, with human review as the gate. That is a guardrail policy, described in his own words.
- CONCRETE EXAMPLES OF PRODUCTIVITY GAINS — he can tell the examples; he cannot yet quantify them (see gaps).

Skills block corroboration, master/upgrad_resume.html section 4: "Hands-on Player-Coach Delivery (AI-Leveraged via Claude Code + OpenAI Codex)", and the headline carries "AI-Leveraged Delivery (Claude Code + OpenAI Codex)".

Why this is worth more than its weight: professional-journey.md line 670 — "It is the most differentiating single item on your résumé for 2026 architect hiring." A required line that most candidates answer with "I use Copilot" is one he answers with a team-wide rollout under a review policy.
scores.gaps:
1. THE MEASUREMENT. professional-journey.md open question 11 (line 724): "Claude Code + Codex — any measurable outcome?" and line 671: "OPEN -> What is the measured outcome? Any before/after on delivery speed, review load, defect rate, or onboarding time?" The JD asks for "concrete examples of productivity gains" — examples he has; a before/after number he does not. Write [fill in metric] and never invent one.
2. A DELIVERY WARNING FROM THE RECORD, not a capability gap. professional-journey.md line 271: at CBRE he said "I'll elaborate on that" about this rollout and then never did. The strongest asset on the résumé was left on the table in the one room where it came up. That is a prep problem, and prep is out of scope here — recorded so it is not lost.
3. GitHub Copilot and Cursor by name are not evidenced. Irrelevant — the JD's list is a "such as", and Claude Code is on it.
scores.ramp_vs_cap:
STRENGTH, not a gap. The single point deducted is for the missing quantified before/after, which is a RECALL AND MEASUREMENT gap rather than a capability one — the rollout happened, the guardrail was a review policy, and the team was ~20 engineers. Do not close it by inventing a percentage.

Worth noting for the level decision: the LEAD document asks only for daily use, gains and guardrails. The PRINCIPAL document asks for "productivity gains, guardrails AND rollout to other engineers", and adds a responsibility — "Set the standard for AI-assisted development across the team, including tooling, prompt and review practices, safety guardrails and measurement of productivity gains." Rollout to other engineers is precisely what he did and precisely what the Lead bar does not pay for. His most differentiating asset is worth more on the Principal document than on this one.
scores.verdict: 9/10. The best-matched line on either document. A required bullet that he answers with a team-wide rollout under an explicit review guardrail, when most candidates answer it with personal tool use.

scores.criterion: sdk-design-versioning-and-distribution — "3+ years designing, versioning and distributing SDKs, including packaging, semantic versioning, PyPI or an internal package registry" (Lead JD, bullet 6); responsibility 2: "Design, develop, test, version and publish Python SDKs, including semantic versioning, strong documentation and practical samples"
scores.evidence:
THE SECOND REAL GAP, AND IT IS UNEVIDENCED RATHER THAN THIN.

Verified directly by grep across killer-query-case-studies/ (~198,000 words), professional-journey.md, master/upgrad_resume.html and both live card dumps: PyPI — zero hits. Semantic versioning / semver — zero hits. Package registry — zero hits. Wheel, setup.py, pyproject — zero hits. The token "SDK" appears exactly twice in the entire case-study corpus, and both times it is a negation: kq10-cross-domain.html, "the one narrative call runs on Llama 3.1 inside the VPC via the native Ollama API — no vendor SDK, no external egress". There is no published-package story to find.

WHAT IS GENUINELY THERE, AND IT IS THE HARDER HALF. The JD's underlying ask is code other teams build on, versioned, without breaking them.
- master/live_card_dump_august_master.json PR-child-1 bullet 2: "Designed shared platform APIs on a multi-tenant SaaS — ... secured 20+ enterprise clients, with strict backward-compatibility discipline." Bullet 14 restates it. Bullet 8: "customer-specific frontends that called a shared Spring Boot backend with API versioning."
- master/upgrad_resume.html section 4 carries "Shared Platform APIs (Contracts, Backward Compatibility)" as a named capability.
- kq7-confidence-calibration.html, on shared libraries: "One implementation of the 90-day outcome labeller and the seeded, cluster-aware bootstrap used across every cohort query in the programme — no per-team reimplementation drift." That is an internal shared Python library consumed across ten pipelines. It is not described as versioned, packaged or published.
- professional-journey.md line 198: authentication, billing/subscription and global configuration built as cross-product services "serving every product in the portfolio" — platform code multiple teams consumed, for five years.
scores.gaps:
1. PACKAGING AND DISTRIBUTION — no evidence, at all, in any form. PyPI, an internal registry, wheels, a release process: none of it is in the record.
2. SEMANTIC VERSIONING as a practice — his versioning evidence is HTTP API versioning at Deque, not package semver with a deprecation policy.
3. DURATION on the SDK-as-a-product discipline: 3+ years required, and there is no window to point at.
4. Documentation and practical samples as SDK deliverables: the closest is Deque bullet 6, "coaching engineers on documentation, code review, and scalable contracts" — real, but about API quality, not about a published SDK.
Do not manufacture any of this. The temptation on this criterion is to let "shared libraries used across ten pipelines" drift into "SDK", and it must not.
scores.ramp_vs_cap:
MIXED, and the halves separate cleanly.

CAPABILITY CAP: "3+ years designing, versioning and distributing SDKs" as a stated minimum, with zero evidence of the distribution half. Nothing in a rewrite closes this.

RAMP ITEM: the mechanics — pyproject.toml, build backends, semver tagging, a PyPI or CodeArtifact publish step. Days of work for an architect who has already run breaking-change management across 20+ enterprise consumers for five years. The hard part of SDK ownership is deciding what breaks whom and when, and that part is evidenced.

The honest sentence for a room: he has owned shared platform interfaces that other teams built on, with backward-compatibility discipline, since 2019 — in Java over HTTP rather than as a published Python package.
scores.verdict: 4/10. Partial credit for the consumer-contract and breaking-change discipline, which is real and multi-year. Zero credit for packaging, semantic versioning and registry distribution, which are absent from the record. This is the second binding constraint after Python duration, and unlike Python it is at least partly a ramp.

scores.ramp_vs_cap: REQUIREMENT SUBSTANTIALLY MET on the CI/CD half; the Python quality toolchain is a RAMP ITEM in the most literal sense — pytest, ruff, black and mypy are configuration, not capability, and an engineer running ten production Python services has almost certainly met them. verdict:
# Adjudication — Wolters Kluwer, LEAD AI Platform Engineer (via Andela)

## TECHNICAL SCORE: 70.9 / 100

Arithmetic, weights summing to 1.00:

    production-python-duration-and-depth   0.16 x  5 = 0.80
    web-apis-in-python-at-scale            0.13 x  6 = 0.78
    production-genai-llm-rag-evaluation    0.14 x  8 = 1.12
    ai-assisted-development                0.10 x  9 = 0.90
    sdk-design-versioning-distribution     0.10 x  4 = 0.40
    cloud-platform-and-iac                 0.10 x  8 = 0.80
    cicd-testing-and-quality-tooling       0.07 x  7 = 0.49
    sql-nosql-and-vector-data-layers       0.07 x  9 = 0.63
    enterprise-security                    0.05 x  9 = 0.45
    observability                          0.04 x  8 = 0.32
    lead-level-technical-ownership         0.04 x 10 = 0.40
                                                       ----
                                           weighted   7.09  ->  70.9 / 100

## THE TARGET IS 95+. THIS DOES NOT REACH IT, AND NOTHING HONEST CLOSES THE GAP.

Two requirements are missed on evidence, not on framing, and between them they carry 26% of the weight:

**1. Production Python — 14 months against a 5+ year minimum.** Mar 2025 to Apr 2026, one window,
no earlier Python role anywhere in nineteen years. This is a DURATION cap. No Rule 7 re-vectoring,
no rewrite, no generous reading of an "e.g." qualifier touches it, because "5+ years of hands-on
production Python" is a stated minimum and not an example list. Lowering the bar from the Principal's
8+ to the Lead's 5+ shrinks the shortfall from 82 months to 46 — it does not convert a fail into a pass.

**2. SDK design, versioning and distribution — 3+ years required, packaging unevidenced entirely.**
Verified by grep across ~198,000 words of case studies, the journey document and both live card dumps:
PyPI, semver, package registry, wheel, setup.py and pyproject all return zero hits. The token "SDK"
appears twice, both times as "no vendor SDK". What he does have is the harder half — five years of
shared platform APIs consumed by 20+ enterprise clients under strict backward-compatibility discipline
and API versioning — which earns partial credit and nothing more.

A third factor is real but not a capability failure: **Azure is strongly preferred and Azure is on the
never-claim list.** The requirement reads "Azure and/or AWS" and roughly nine years of AWS with
Terraform satisfies it outright, so it costs two points on one criterion and is named as a real-world
gate rather than scored as a gap.

## WHAT IS GENUINELY STRONG, AND SHOULD LEAD

**The AI-assisted development line, 9/10, and it is rare.** A REQUIRED bullet on both documents asks
for daily use of GitHub Copilot, Cursor or Claude Code with concrete productivity gains and the
guardrails applied. He answers it with a Claude Code and OpenAI Codex rollout across a ~20-engineer
team, scoped deliberately to architectural exploration, first-cut implementations and test scaffolding,
with hands-on review as the gate. Most candidates answer this line with personal tool use. The one
thing missing is the measured before/after, which professional-journey.md open question 11 still asks
and which must be written [fill in metric], never invented.

**Production GenAI, 8/10** — the closest he comes to any duration bar on this document, 14 months
against 24. RAG on Elasticsearch dense_vector filtered kNN across 80+ chronic conditions with
Neptune deliberately off the serving path; self-hosted Llama 3.1 8B/70B in-VPC under HIPAA with
uncertainty-gated escalation to the larger model; LangChain model seam; LangGraph with Postgres
checkpoints; guardrails, golden sets and offline eval; self-hosted LangSmith for tracing.

**Enterprise security, 9/10 and no duration bar on it** — ~300 instances migrated from isolated
Keycloak to central Red Hat single sign-on with zero end-user disruption, OIDC and OAuth 2.0 across
realms, clients, roles and groups, tenancy resolved from the JWT on every request.

**Data layers, 9/10** — nineteen years of SQL, OpenSearch in a production request path at 13-23 calls
per message, and OpenSearch is one of the three vector stores the JD names by name.

**Regulated B2B fit** — Wolters Kluwer sells legal, tax, health and compliance information, and the
Lead JD's first Nice-to-Have names exactly that. HIPAA across ten pipelines, PHI contained in-VPC,
regulated banks on carved-out infrastructure inside an ISO 27001 environment. This is not a scored
criterion and it is one of the better reasons the seat suits him.

## PRINCIPAL vs LEAD — THE CALL

Scored on identical weights against the Principal document's higher thresholds, the same evidence
comes out at **65.8 / 100** (Python 4, Web APIs 5, GenAI 7, observability 7 for the added SLI/SLO
clause, scope 9; everything else unchanged). So the Lead rubric scores **5.1 points higher**.

**Apply for the PRINCIPAL anyway.** The rubric measures distance to a threshold; the decision turns
on where his evidence is worth the most, and those are different questions.

**The reason the score is misleading here:** the binding constraint is IDENTICAL on both documents and
neither bar is met. Fourteen months of Python fails 5+ exactly as it fails 8+. Dropping a level does
not convert the one line that gates him — it only makes the shortfall smaller while giving away
everything he is strongest at.

**And the Principal document is where his strengths are priced in:**

- Its extra responsibility — *"Own the architecture of the AI platform end-to-end, including
  target-state design, technology selection, migration path and technical standards"* — is a literal
  description of his last decade. The Lead document has no counterpart.
- Its AI-assistant bullet asks for productivity gains, guardrails **and rollout to other engineers**.
  Rollout across ~20 engineers is his single most differentiating asset, and the Lead bullet does not
  ask for it. His best card scores full value only on the Principal.
- The six "Your Skills" traits are the clearest tell. Principal's **Platform Architect** — reasoning
  about *"compatibility, versioning, blast radius and total cost of ownership"* — is swapped on the
  Lead document for **Bias for Action**: *"deploy production code quickly using the toolchain
  provided."* One seat defines the toolchain; the other consumes it. He is the first.
- Principal's scope bullet — ownership of a platform or service family used by multiple engineering
  teams, with architectural decisions, trade-offs and **measured outcomes** — he meets squarely, and
  he has the measured outcomes to attach: deploy time to under 10 minutes, infrastructure cost down
  25-30%, error rate under 3%, 46% ELK cost reduction, 50% faster releases. The Lead bullet asks for
  direction over *"a feature area or service"*, which he over-clears by several levels — evidence
  spent for nothing.
- Total experience: 19+ years reads as a Principal candidate short on Python years. Against a 7+ year
  Lead bar it reads as a nineteen-year architect applying down, which invites a second awkward
  question on top of the Python one.
- Principal alone carries a **Preferred Background** section naming IIT, NIT, BITS and **IIIT** — he
  holds a PG Diploma in AI/ML from IIIT Bangalore (Jan 2021) — and that section says outright these
  are *"preferences rather than absolute gates"*. On the Lead document, which has no such section,
  that asset is worth nothing.

**The practical shape:** one recruiter, Paul Abbott at Andela, holds both requisitions. Go in at
Principal with the Python duration named honestly and unprompted-by-them, and let HIM down-level to
Lead if the client pushes back on years. That costs one conversation and keeps the Principal framing
available; opening at Lead forecloses it and cannot be walked back upward.

**Where the Lead argument would win, and it is worth stating plainly:** if the screen is mechanical —
Andela filtering CVs against the stated minimums before a human reads one — Lead is the only document
he could plausibly survive, and even that is not certain, since 14 months fails 5+ as well. If Paul
Abbott indicates the filter is automated rather than conversational, that changes the answer.

## WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE THE GAP — nothing, and that is the honest finding

There is no honest lift here. The smallest genuine lift on most rubrics is Rule 7 re-vectoring of real
work, and it does not apply: the shortfall is elapsed time on two criteria, not the framing of what he
did. Re-vectoring can make the fourteen months read as densely as they deserve — ten production
services, statistical rigour, leakage-safe machine learning, tenant isolation under HIPAA — and that
is worth doing. It moves the room's impression. It does not move the number.

**Apply anyway.** Honesty governs résumé content, never whether to apply. Two required lines are
short; one required line — AI-assisted development with team rollout and guardrails — he answers
better than almost anyone who will apply, and the regulated-B2B fit is direct.
